introduction-less-is-more.core: WireGuard is a VPN protocol of about 4,000 lines of kernel code, against hundreds of thousands for OpenVPN or IPsec stacks. It has no cipher negotiation, no certificates and no complex state machine: peers are identified by public keys, cryptography is fixed and modern, and configuration is a few lines. The small surface is easier to audit, faster, and harder to misconfigure.

first_principles.problem: A team's IPsec configuration has 40 parameters, and every outage involves a negotiation mismatch.

analogy.title: A key-and-lock vs a security committee
analogy.story: Instead of negotiating rules each time, you either have the right key or you don't.
analogy.breaks: Physical keys can be copied visibly; private keys must be protected digitally.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A complete, secure tunnel in ~10 lines.

check.q: Why is WireGuard's lack of cipher negotiation a security advantage?
check.a: It eliminates downgrade attacks and misconfiguration from mismatched or weak cipher choices.

the-opinionated-protocol-noise-fixed-cry.core: WireGuard's handshake uses the Noise_IK pattern. Curve25519 for key exchange, ChaCha20-Poly1305 for authenticated encryption, BLAKE2s for hashing, SipHash for hashtables, and HKDF for key derivation. A one-round-trip handshake establishes session keys with forward secrecy and identity hiding, and keys rotate every 2 minutes. If an algorithm is ever broken, the protocol version changes; there's nothing to negotiate.

first_principles.problem: Auditors ask which cipher suites the VPN might negotiate under attack, and the answer for IPsec is a long list.

analogy.title: A sealed recipe nobody can change
analogy.story: Every kitchen uses the same proven recipe; if it's ever found flawed, a new edition replaces it entirely.
analogy.breaks: Recipes don't expire; WireGuard keys rotate every 2 minutes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Adds symmetric layer against future quantum attacks on Curve25519.

code.text:
wg genpsk > peer1.psk
wg set wg0 peer xTIBA5rbo...= preshared-key ./peer1.psk
wg show wg0 latest-handshakes

check.q: What is the optional PresharedKey in WireGuard for?
check.a: An extra symmetric secret mixed into the handshake, hedging against future (e.g. quantum) breaks of Curve25519.

cryptokey-routing-the-core-innovation.core: Each WireGuard peer has a public key and an AllowedIPs list. Outbound, the destination IP selects the peer whose AllowedIPs contains it (longest match), and the packet is encrypted to that key. Inbound, after decryption, the source IP must fall within the sending peer's AllowedIPs or the packet is dropped. Routing and access control become one table: key ↔ IP ranges.

first_principles.problem: A spoofed packet claiming to be from another peer's subnet must be rejected.
truths: IP ranges define what each peer may send and receive.
derivation: Inbound: **src IP must match** sender's AllowedIPs.

analogy.title: A mail room where each locked mailbox only accepts letters for its residents
analogy.story: Letters are delivered to the box whose residents match the address, and letters claiming to come from a resident are only accepted with their key.
analogy.breaks: Mailrooms can make exceptions; cryptokey routing never does.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 10.1/16 traffic only to/from office key; spoofing impossible.

code.text:
[Peer]   # office
PublicKey = OFFICE_PUB=
AllowedIPs = 10.1.0.0/16
Endpoint = office.example.com:51820

[Peer]   # datacenter
PublicKey = DC_PUB=
AllowedIPs = 10.2.0.0/16
Endpoint = dc.example.com:51820

check.q: What happens if a peer sends a decrypted packet with a source IP outside its AllowedIPs?
check.a: WireGuard drops it, preventing that peer from spoofing other addresses.

statelessness-and-silence.core: WireGuard is silent by default: it doesn't respond to unauthenticated packets at all, so port scanners see nothing. It's effectively stateless from the user's view: no connection to 'bring up'; handshakes happen on demand when there's traffic and keys expire automatically. Peers roam freely, since the endpoint updates to the latest authenticated source address. PersistentKeepalive keeps NAT mappings alive for peers behind NAT.

first_principles.problem: A laptop moves from Wi-Fi to 4G, and the VPN must keep working without reconnecting.
truths: Authenticated packets prove identity wherever they come from.

analogy.title: A door with no bell that only opens for the right key
analogy.story: Strangers knocking get no answer; the owner can arrive at any entrance and walk in.
analogy.breaks: Doors don't time out; NAT mappings do, hence keepalives.

code.text:
wg show wg0 endpoints
# PEER_PUB=  203.0.113.50:41022   (Wi-Fi)
# ...switch to 4G...
wg show wg0 endpoints
# PEER_PUB=  198.51.100.77:60311  (cellular) — updated automatically

check.q: Why does WireGuard need PersistentKeepalive behind NAT?
check.a: Without periodic traffic, the NAT mapping expires, and inbound packets from the other peer can't reach the client.

modern-meshes-tailscale-and-netmaker.core: WireGuard leaves key distribution, peer discovery and NAT traversal to you. Mesh products add a control plane: Tailscale (and the open-source Headscale) or Netmaker distribute keys and peer lists via SSO-authenticated coordination servers, perform NAT traversal (STUN, hole punching, DERP relays), push ACLs and DNS (MagicDNS), and give every device direct encrypted paths to every other, a zero-trust overlay.

first_principles.problem: Manually managing WireGuard keys and AllowedIPs for 300 devices across homes, offices and clouds is unmanageable.
truths: WireGuard is a data plane only.
derivation: Use **subnet routers/exit nodes** for legacy networks.

analogy.title: A switchboard that introduces callers then steps aside
analogy.story: It tells each phone how to reach the other directly, and only patches the call through itself if a direct line can't be made.
analogy.breaks: Switchboards hear calls; Tailscale relays only see encrypted packets.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only SREs reach prod SSH/HTTPS; direct encrypted paths.

check.q: What is a DERP relay used for in Tailscale?
check.a: Relaying encrypted WireGuard traffic when NAT traversal fails to establish a direct peer-to-peer path.
